metadata.title: It Looked Complete
metadata.source_commit_subject: snickerdoodle: gate records carry their own evidence
metadata.series_position: episode 9 — a record that looked complete and did not carry its evidence
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 9, from the last pushed commit on feat/gate-records (93485c4; origin contains it and the branch is in sync). FRAMEWORK: three questions for any audit record — DOES IT NAME WHAT IT LOOKED AT / CAN IT TELL ABSENT FROM UNKNOWABLE / IS A DEFAULT VISIBLY A DEFAULT. Falsifiability beat is B08, the UTC date bug: a decision made on 22 Oct was recorded as the 23rd, in a record whose purpose is who decided what and when. The 26 JSON files were recounted from the committed tree; the commit's '2 to 32 evidence files' could NOT be reproduced (I count 31 under those two trees) and is therefore not shown on screen — see FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. The command I built last week writes a decision record every time a human clears a gate. The records looked fine. Then I put one next to the ones a human had written by hand, and five fields were simply missing.

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "diff the record my gate command writes against the ones written by hand"
output: and the date was the wrong day

beats.role_note: series continuity — last week built the command; this week reads what it wrote
beats.narration_text: Last episode built the command that runs steps and records gate decisions. It worked. But a record written by a machine and a record written by a person are not automatically the same thing, and the only way to find out was to put them side by side. Five fields were absent, and one more was present but meaningless — residual risk, filled with a generic default where the human had written the actual specifics.

shot.show: machine record beside hand record, with the five absent fields marked
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered panels side by side. Left, the machine record, in soft ink. Right, the hand-written one, taller. Between them a terracotta column lists the five field names that appear only on the right, with residual_risk marked separately as present-but-generic.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any audit record, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any record that claims something was checked. One: does it name what it looked at — not a summary, the actual files. Two: can it tell absent from unknowable — because writing not found when you mean cannot tell is a false statement, not a gap. Three: is a default visibly a default — or does boilerplate end up reading as somebody's judgment.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: DOES IT NAME WHAT IT LOOKED AT / ABSENT OR UNKNOWABLE / IS A DEFAULT VISIBLE
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The second lands in terracotta — it is the distinction this episode turns on — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.narration_text: The ask was to make the record carry its own evidence, instead of asserting that evidence exists somewhere.

shot.show: the composer with the evidence ask

props.command: claude "make each gate record name and hash the files its own test actually points at"

beats.role_note: QUESTION 1 — name what you looked at. The depth bug, with the verified count.
beats.narration_text: Question one. The evidence list is derived from the gate's own test, not from a list I choose — if the test names a path, that path is what the gate is about, and it gets hashed so a reader can confirm what was judged. The first version stopped at the top level. Gate three's test names two directories whose real contents sit two levels down, so hashing stopped at the children and missed every one of the twenty-six JSON files the gate exists to check.
beats.new_visual_element: the depth bug and what it skipped

shot.show: a directory walked to depth 1 versus walked fully, and the 26 JSON files
shot.visual_intent: Left: a small tree drawn two levels deep with a terracotta line marking where the first version stopped, with everything below it drawn but unhashed. Right: a stat card reading 26 JSON files, captioned 'what the gate exists to check'. Citation strip names the recount command.

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — gate 3's test, from the committed recipe
beats.narration_text: Here is the test itself, out of the recipe. It names two directories and asks every JSON beneath them to parse. The paths in that line are the evidence list. Nothing else needed to be decided.

shot.show: the gate 3 test line as committed

props.title: recipes/market-sentiment-analysis-part-1.md  @ 93485c4
props.code:
3. Data-shape gate: Every raw and verified JSON
   output parses before downstream scripts run.

   Test:
     find data/raw/market-sentiment-analysis-part-1 \
          data/verified/market-sentiment-analysis-part-1 \
          -name "*.json" -print \
          -exec python3 -m json.tool {} \;

   Human capacity: [PA].

   # the two paths in this line ARE the evidence list.
props.sparkLine: The test already said what the gate is about

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — absent versus unknowable, the distinction the record now makes
beats.narration_text: Question two, and this is the one worth taking away. Some tokens in a test are not file paths at all. Gate four's test loops over a list of names. Gate six's contains a date template in square brackets. If the record writes exists false for those, it asserts that a file is missing when no such file was ever meant to exist. So it writes resolved false, with a note saying it cannot tell a loop value from a template from a genuinely missing file. That is a smaller claim, and it is the true one.
beats.new_visual_element: the two kinds of not-found, separated

shot.show: exists:false versus resolved:false, with the two real examples
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows. The first, in soft ink, shows exists:false with the words 'asserts a file is missing'. The second, terracotta, shows resolved:false with 'cannot distinguish a loop value from a template'. Beneath, two small chips name the real cases: gate 4's loop, gate 6's [DATE].

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 — a default must look like a default, and a check must not read as an assertion
beats.narration_text: Question three. The record now marks whether a human actually supplied the residual risk, so a default is visibly a default instead of passing as someone's judgment. The run log field became a check rather than an assertion — it looks for a dated entry and records whether one exists, so a record can never point at a log entry nobody wrote. And mode and scope are read out of the run envelope instead of assumed.
beats.new_visual_element: the three fields that changed from assertion to observation

shot.show: residual_risk_stated / run_log as a check / mode and scope read from the envelope
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered rows, each showing a field name and what it now records. Each carries a small chip reading 'observed' in ink where the old behaviour would have read 'assumed' in terracotta.

beats.role_note: the date bug — the sharpest self-caught error, in a record whose point is when
beats.narration_text: And then the one that makes the point better than anything I planned. The timestamp used the standard ISO function, which returns UTC. A decision made on the twenty-second of October, late in the evening, was recorded as the twenty-third. One day off, in a record whose entire purpose is to say who decided what, and when. Everything else in this commit is about evidence being real. The date field was quietly wrong the whole time.
beats.new_visual_element: the UTC offset, and the field it corrupted

shot.show: a decision made on the 22nd, recorded as the 23rd
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards. Left: 'decided' with 22 Oct in ink. Right: 'recorded' with 23 Oct in terracotta. A short connector between them carries the label toISOString() returns UTC. Beneath, one line: the record exists to say who decided what, and when.

beats.role_note: what was verified after the change — including that nothing else moved
beats.narration_text: Verified after the change. All six gates now produce different evidence sets, which is the point — if they all produced the same list, the list would not be coming from the tests. The four refusal paths from last week still hold: a failing test, a live gate without its second flag, a missing note, an overwrite without force. Run and check are unaffected, and the repository's own verify still passes.
beats.new_visual_element: the post-change checks, including the unchanged ones

shot.show: six distinct evidence sets / four refusals still hold / run and check unaffected
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered groups stacked. The first shows six small distinct bars labelled gate 1 to 6. The second lists the four refusal paths with drawn ticks. The third, a single row, confirms run, check and verify unchanged — in soft ink, because 'nothing moved' is the quiet half of a verification.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own audit trail, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open any record your systems write when something is approved or checked, and ask what it names. If it says a check passed but not what it opened, it is a claim about a claim. And look at its timestamp — ask whose day that is.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator
